blocks.prompt: 23. If the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of a progression is a linear expression in \(n\), then prove that this progression is an A.P.
blocks.explanation:
A general proof. 'Linear in \(n\)' means \(a_n = An + B\) for fixed numbers \(A\) and \(B\).
A progression is an A.P. when \(a_{n+1} - a_n\) is the same for every \(n\).
Plan: compute \(a_{n+1} - a_n\) and show it does not depend on \(n\).
steps:
Given: \(a_n = An + B\) (\(A, B\) constants)
To prove: the progression is an A.P.
Method: Show that the difference of consecutive terms is a constant.

Write \(a_{n+1}\)
\[a_{n+1} = A(n + 1) + B\]
\[= An + A + B\]
Why: Replace \(n\) by \(n + 1\).

Find the difference
\[a_{n+1} - a_n = (An + A + B) - (An + B)\]
\[= A\]
Why: \(An\) and \(B\) cancel.

Conclude
\[a_1 = A + B,\quad d = A\]
Why: The difference \(A\) is the same for every \(n\), so the progression is an A.P. with first term \(A + B\) and common difference \(A\).

Check with an example
\(a_n = 4 + 3n\) (Question 3): \(7, 10, 13, \ldots\)
\[d = 3 = A \;\checkmark\]
Why: The coefficient of \(n\) is the common difference.
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(a_n = An + B\) gives an A.P. with \(d = A\) and \(a_1 = A + B\).
